During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy.

The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server.

This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.

Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

Introducing QwenGyre, bringing elastic RL to extreme-long-horizon (XLong) agent training. ✨

It launches with two core designs: 🥳
- Elastic Scheduler: reallocates GPUs between rollout & training as demand shifts—live executions never interrupted. Up to 1.85× speedup over Colocate, 1.78× over Async.
- Trajectory Processor: turns branching executions (compaction, sub-agents, retries) into prefix-shared trajectory trees with bounded, deduplicated training samples. Partial progress after timeout still gets scored.

Scaled to Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B with ~700K tokens per rollout, QwenGyre lifts NL2RepoBench from 52.5% to 58.5% in 48 steps, cutting end-to-end training time by ~44% vs Async.

That was the duration of Ariane 6’s longest mission to date, the launch of Galileo satellites 33 and 34 in December 2025.

A mission stretching nearly four hours is not just a number. It reflects the precision required to deliver two navigation satellites into their exact orbital slots, with multiple powered phases, coast phases and a highly accurate upper stage re-ignition sequence.

A powerful demonstration of Ariane 6's ability to carry out complex orbital deployments.

For Galileo, precision is essential.

And it starts at launch.

🚀 How do we make sure a spacecraft will fit perfectly with Ariane 6?

Before integration with the launcher in French Guiana, teams check the interface between the spacecraft and its launch adapter.

The adapter forms the mechanical and electrical connection between the spacecraft and Ariane 6. It keeps the spacecraft securely attached during launch and enables its separation once the intended orbit has been reached.

During the fit check, teams verify that the spacecraft and its adapter match perfectly, which is a key step before moving forward with the launch campaign.

Once these checks are complete, the spacecraft can move on to the next stage of its preparation for launch.

27 minutes with Ariane 5. 8 years to reach Mercury. 🚀

On 20 October 2018, BepiColombo lifted off from Europe’s Spaceport aboard Ariane 5.

Around 27 minutes later, the spacecraft separated from the launcher and began the next stage of its journey: an eight-year voyage through the inner Solar System to reach Mercury.

A few minutes with Ariane 5 were the first step in a journey lasting billions of kilometres.

From launch to separation, every minute was about putting BepiColombo on the right path for what came next.

📣 Announcement: ispace has been selected by JAXA as a contractor for its competitive proposal solicitation, “Conceptual Design for the Realization of a Lunar Solar Power Tower (Parts A-B)"

As lunar activities continue to expand, a stable power supply will be a critical component of the infrastructure needed to enable sustained operations on the lunar surface, with a projected requirement on the order of tens of kilowatts (kW) by the early 2030s. 

ispace will proceed with arrangements to finalize a contract with JAXA and will work with partner companies on the conceptual design of the lunar solar power tower and its power distribution system for lunar surface equipment. Drawing on the expertise and experience gained through its lunar exploration missions and lander development programs, ispace will contribute to defining system requirements and specifications, interfaces with lunar landers, and plans for future development.

“As activities on the lunar surface gain momentum, developing essential infrastructure—including power, communications, and positioning capabilities—will become increasingly important alongside transportation. We are very pleased to have the opportunity to participate in JAXA’s conceptual design initiative for a lunar solar power tower," said Takeshi Hakamada, Founder & CEO, ispace, inc.

📣 Announcement: ispace and ArianeGroup (@ArianeGroup) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to expand our strategic collaboration supporting the development of current and future lunar spacecraft and missions. 🤝🌕

Building on our longstanding relationship, ispace has selected ArianeGroup pulsing thrusters and reaction control system (RCS) thruster hardware for integration into its ULTRA lunar landers. ArianeGroup is also contracted to provide related assembly, integration, and testing (AIT) services in support of the development.

Under the new MOU, our companies will explore opportunities to expand this collaboration beyond ULTRA, including future lunar spacecraft and missions across ispace’s global organization, while evaluating long-term cooperation to support stable lander production and our targeted mission cadence.

The agreement was signed today at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Türkiye.
